notes.title: Vectors and the dot product
Matrix multiplication, computed
Solving linear systems
notes.body: Worked example: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2. Add the equations: 3x = 9, so x = **3**; then y = 7 − 2×3 = **1**. Check: 2×3+1 = 7 ✓; 3−1 = 2 ✓. Elimination is the algorithm; the geometry is two lines intersecting at one point. A system has a unique solution exactly when the coefficient matrix is invertible (nonzero determinant).

notes.title: Determinant and invertibility
notes.body: For 2×2 [[a,b],[c,d]], det = ad − bc. Worked: A=[[1, 2], [3, 4]], det = 1×4 − 2×3 = **-2**. Nonzero → invertible → the system Ax=b has exactly one solution. det = 0 means the rows are dependent: the map crushes a dimension (area → 0). |det| is the area-scaling factor of the transformation. Singular matrices (det 0) are why 'matrix is singular' errors appear — the inverse doesn't exist.

notes.title: Describing data, computed
Probability rules
notes.body: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B|A); for independent events, P(A)·P(B). P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B). Worked example: two independent deploys each fail with p=0.1. P(both fail) = 0.1×0.1 = **0.010000000000000002**. P(at least one fails) = 1 − P(neither) = 1 − 0.9² = **0.19**. Complement-first ('1 minus the boring case') solves most 'at least one' problems. Independence is an assumption to check, not a default: correlated failures break the multiplication.

notes.title: Conditional probability and Bayes
Expectation
notes.body: E[X] = Σ x·P(x): the long-run average. Worked example: a retry policy succeeds on attempt 1 with p=0.7, attempt 2 with p=0.2, attempt 3 with p=0.1 (then gives up). Expected attempts = 1×0.7 + 2×0.2 + 3×0.1 = **1.4000000000000001**. Linearity of expectation: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even when X,Y are dependent — the workhorse for analyzing total cost, total latency, total errors across components without modeling their joint distribution.

notes.title: Sets and the inclusion–exclusion principle
Counting: product and sum rules
notes.body: Product rule: if a task has a choices for step 1 and b for step 2, there are a×b combined outcomes. Sum rule: for disjoint alternatives, add. Worked example: a password of 2 letters then 3 digits. Letters: 26^2 = 676; digits: 10^3 = 1000; total = 676,000 by the product rule. Worked example 2: an identifier is either a 3-letter code or a 4-digit code: 26^3 + 10^4 = 27,576 by the sum rule (disjoint cases). Name the rule before computing — most counting errors are rule-selection errors, not arithmetic.

notes.title: Permutations and combinations, computed
The pigeonhole principle
Induction, with a verified example
Recurrences and divide-and-conquer cost
notes.body: Worked example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n with T(1) = 1 (the mergesort shape). Unfold: each level does n work across twice as many subproblems; there are log2(n) levels. Closed form: T(n) = n·log2(n) + n. Verification at n=1024: recursion computes **11264**, closed form gives 1024·10+1024 = **11264** — exact match. This is where n log n comes from, not from memorization: count the levels, multiply by work per level. Every divide-and-conquer analysis in this course follows this template.

objectives: Apply inclusion–exclusion to overlapping counts.
Choose correctly between permutations and combinations and compute both.
Prove closed forms by induction with explicit base and step.

notes.title: Worked example: Which of the following is a topic covered in "Python Core Syntax"?
notes.body:
**Problem.** Which of the following is a topic covered in "Python Core Syntax"?

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Control flow: if, for, while
- **Why:** "Control flow: if, for, while" is listed among this module's topics; the other options come from different modules.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *"Control flow: if, for, while" is listed among this module's topics; the other options come from different modules.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Honesty note
Worked example: Which of the following is a topic covered in "Objects, Modules, and…
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Objects, Modules, and Environments, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

Hands-on procedure
notes.code:
import time, concurrent.futures

def fetch(i):
    time.sleep(0.2)  # stand-in for network I/O
    return i * i

t0 = time.perf_counter()
seq = [fetch(i) for i in range(20)]
t1 = time.perf_counter()
with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as ex:
    par = list(ex.map(fetch, range(20)))
t2 = time.perf_counter()
print(f'sequential {t1-t0:.2f}s  threaded {t2-t1:.2f}s')

modules.summary: Welcome to the module the original program's marketing glosses over. I'm your instructor, and this is the GenAI-Assisted Coding Workflow: drafting Python with a language model, executing and verifying everything it generates, treating tests as the contract instead of trust, debugging with AI assistance, and — the skill that matters most — knowing when the model is wrong. The honest loop is prompt, generate, execute, verify. Anyone can do the first two; professionals live in the last two.

Hands-on procedure
notes.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)          # seeded generator
X = rng.standard_normal((1000, 20))       # 1000 samples, 20 features
z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)  # z-score along the sample axis
mask = (z[:, 0] > 2.0)                   # boolean mask on feature 0
print(z.shape, mask.sum(), 'outliers in feature 0')

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Build an array-powered data profiler: given a CSV of numeric data, load it with NumPy, and report per-column mean, std, min, max, and outlier counts (|z| > 3) — all vectorized, no Python loops over rows. Add a seeded 80/20 train/test split function and a one-line timing comparison of your vectorized column stats versus a pure-Python loop version. Grading bar: on a 1M-row file your vectorized path must finish in seconds while the loop version visibly crawls — and your report must state the measured speedup factor. If any loop touches rows, it fails.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: NumPy fluency is infrastructure, not a credential — this module confers none, and array programming alone doesn't make you a data scientist. The durable wins are shape literacy (read the shape before the traceback) and the vectorization reflex. Random-seed discipline matters for your own reproducibility; it doesn't make results 'more correct'.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv', parse_dates=['order_date'])

    df[df['status'] == 'complete']

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Wrangle-to-model-ready: take two messy CSVs (orders + customers, with mismatched key formats, missing values, a wide-format monthly table, and dirty date strings) and produce a single tidy, model-ready table plus a wrangling report. The report documents every decision: join type and row-count audit, missing-data handling per column with mechanism justification, tidy transformations applied, and dtypes chosen. Grading bar: I run your script on a variant of the data with new dirty rows — it must not crash, and the report must let me reproduce every decision. Chained assignment anywhere is an automatic fail.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Wrangling is labor, not magic: no pandas trick fixes data that was never collected, and missing-data handling is a judgment call, not a formula — document the mechanism assumption. This module confers no certificate. The durable skill is the audit habit: check shapes, counts, and dtypes after every transformation, because silent corruption is the default failure mode of data pipelines.

**Problem.** Which practice prevents leakage?

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Preprocessing inside the pipeline, inside the fold
- **Why:** Every preprocessing step inside the pipeline, inside the fold - or the scores are fiction.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Every preprocessing step inside the pipeline, inside the fold - or the scores are fiction.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Visualization, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

Hands-on procedure
notes.code:
-- Validation gate: null rates + key cardinality
WITH base AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders
)
SELECT
  (SELECT n FROM base) AS rows,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE customer_id IS NULL) * 1.0 / (SELECT n FROM base) AS null_customer_rate,
  COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS distinct_orders
FROM orders;

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In SQL for AI Engineers: Analytical Queries and Dataset Validation, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Supervised Learning, these are the recurring traps:

**Problem.** Which of the following is a topic covered in "Validation and Hyperparameter Tuning"?

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Stratified splits for classification

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *"Stratified splits for classification" is listed among this module's topics; the other options come from different modules.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Validation and Hyperparameter Tuning, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

cards.back: On imbalanced data - 99% accuracy is trivial when 99% of labels are negative. Choose the metric that matches the business cost.

cards.front: What is the F1 score?
cards.back: The harmonic mean of precision and recall - a single number balancing both.

cards.front: What does ROC-AUC measure?

cards.back: MAE: average absolute error. RMSE: square root of mean squared error - punishes large errors more.

import numpy as np

def relu(x): return np.maximum(0, x)

# 2 -> 3 -> 1 network, forward pass by hand
W1 = np.array([[0.5, -0.2, 0.1], [0.3, 0.8, -0.4]])
b1 = np.zeros(3)

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *"Universal approximation: what depth buys you" is listed among this module's topics; the other options come from different modules.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Neural Network Foundations, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Optimization is half science, half craft: the theory explains the loss curves you'll see, but the learning rate still gets tuned empirically. Adam 'just works' as a default — the honest caveat is that well-tuned SGD sometimes generalizes better, and defaults are starting points, not answers. This module confers no certificate; the durable skill is reading loss and gradient traces like instruments.

notes.title: Project brief
Honesty note
notes.body: CNNs are the right bias for images, not a universal vision solution — transformers now compete in vision too, and the 'classic architectures' are ideas to learn from, not relics to memorize. Transfer learning is powerful but not magic: pretraining on natural images helps natural-image tasks most, and domain gaps (medical, satellite) shrink the benefit. No certificate is conferred.

Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Convolutional Networks, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

cards.front: How do you do early stopping 'done right'?
cards.back: Monitor validation loss, not training loss. Keep the best checkpoint (patience on no improvement). Never peek at the test set to decide when to stop - that turns the test set into a validation set.

for epoch in range(epochs):

notes.title: Worked example: Precision vs recall:
notes.body:
**Problem.** Precision vs recall:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Precision = of predicted positives, how many were right; recall = of actual positives, how many were found
- **Why:** Precision punishes false alarms; recall punishes misses.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Precision punishes false alarms; recall punishes misses.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Worked example: Why did attention replace recurrence?
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Transformers and Attention, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

notes.title: Concepts
Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Train the classics on toy data and watch their pathologies firsthand. Small, fast, instructive.
1. **Sample from a learned distribution.** Fit a simple density model to 2D toy data; sample from it and compare samples to training data. 'Learning a distribution' made concrete before any neural net.
2. **Build a VAE.** Encoder-decoder with the reparameterization trick on a toy image dataset; visualize the latent space (2D) colored by class. Watch structure emerge in z.
3. **Interpolate the latent space.** Walk between two latent codes and decode the path; observe smooth morphing. The famous demo, reproduced — and note where it breaks.
4. **Build a GAN.** Generator vs discriminator on the same toy data; plot both losses. Observe the delicate balance — then deliberately unbalance it (too-strong discriminator) and watch training die.
5. **Induce mode collapse.** Constrain or mistune the GAN until it produces limited variety; measure diversity collapse quantitatively (e.g. per-class counts). The pathology, induced and measured.
6. **Anomaly-detect with a VAE.** Train on normal data only; flag high-reconstruction-error samples as anomalies. A VAE use case that survives the diffusion era.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Generative-families report: train a VAE and a GAN on the same toy image dataset I provide, and deliver samples from both, latent-space visualizations with interpolations, a mode-collapse stress test with diversity metrics, and a writeup comparing the families' strengths, failure modes, and surviving use cases. Grading bar: the report must show at least one failure from each family (collapse, blurry VAE samples) with diagnosis — a report of two perfect models is fiction.

notes.title: Worked example: Which of the following is a topic covered in "Diffusion and…
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Diffusion and Image/Video Generation, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

notes.title: Concepts
Hands-on procedure
notes.code:
def rag_answer(question, db, llm, k=4):
    chunks = db.similarity_search(question, k=k)   # retrieve
    context = '

'.join(c.text for c in chunks)
    prompt = ('Answer using ONLY the context below. '
              'Cite chunk numbers. If unanswerable, say so.

'
              f'Context:
{context}

Question: {question}')
    return llm.complete(prompt), [c.id for c in chunks]

Grading bar: any factual answer without a citation fails — and the evaluation must include questions the corpus can't answer, with the system's behavior documented.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: RAG grounds generation in your data; it doesn't make the model truthful — retrieval quality bounds answer quality, and confident confabulation survives bad retrieval. cards.front: Why is the distance metric a first-class design decision in a vector database?
cards.back: Cosine vs. dot product vs. Euclidean changes which neighbors count as 'near'. The metric must match the embedding model's training geometry - mismatch it and retrieval silently degrades.

cards.front: When does accuracy lie?
cards.back: On imbalanced data - 99% accuracy is trivial when 99% of labels are negative. Choose the metric that matches the business cost.

cards.front: What does a vector database index?
cards.back: Embeddings for approximate nearest-neighbor search - e.g., HNSW graphs trading recall, latency, and memory.

cards.front: What does cosine similarity measure?
cards.back: The angle between two vectors - direction, not magnitude.

cards.front: Cosine vs dot product vs Euclidean: when?

cards.front: Precision vs recall:
cards.back: **Precision = of predicted positives, how many were right; recall = of actual positives, how many were found** — Precision punishes false alarms; recall punishes misses.

notes.body: Vector-index selection report: on a corpus I provide with a fixed query set and relevance judgments, benchmark at least three index configurations end to end (recall@k, p99 latency, memory), include the hybrid + rerank pipeline, and deliver the engine recommendation with the tradeoff table and sizing math for 10x scale. notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Vector search is approximate by design — 'nearest' means 'nearest the index found', and recall is the honesty metric. Benchmarks on one corpus don't transfer to another; your data, your queries, your measurements. This module confers no certificate; the durable skill is the benchmark discipline: recall, latency, and memory reported together, always.

cards.front: When does GraphRAG beat plain vector retrieval?
cards.back: Multi-hop questions over related entities: the knowledge graph traverses relationships (A to B to C) that no single chunk contains. Vector search finds similar text; GraphRAG finds connected facts.

cards.front: Why build baselines before complexity?

cards.front: What do LoRA rank and alpha control?
cards.back: Rank sets the adapter's capacity - low means few trainable parameters. Alpha scales the adapter's influence. Typical starts: rank 8-16, alpha at 2x rank. Too low underfits; too high wastes the efficiency.

cards.front: What is catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuning?
cards.back: Aggressive fine-tuning overwrites pretrained knowledge. Mitigations: low ranks, small learning rates, keeping general data in the mix, and re-evaluating base capabilities after tuning.

cards.front: QLoRA adds what on top of LoRA?
cards.back: **A 4-bit quantized base model** — 4-bit base weights plus adapters - fine-tuning large models on a single GPU.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Fine-tuning report: fine-tune a small open model with LoRA/QLoRA on a task dataset I provide. Deliver the run configuration (rank/alpha/targets with justification), the trainable-parameter accounting, quality-vs-rank sweep results, forgetting regression checks, and the head-to-head evaluation against a RAG baseline on the same task with the build recommendation. Grading bar: the recommendation must cite the head-to-head numbers — and any tuned model shipped without forgetting checks fails.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Fine-tuning changes behavior, not knowledge — it won't reliably inject fast-changing facts (that's RAG's job), and small datasets teach memorization, not skill. QLoRA specifics are as of 2026-10-07; libraries evolve. This module confers no certificate; the durable skill is the comparison discipline: same task, both approaches, measured honestly.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Multimodal Foundation Models, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

cards.front: The RLHF pipeline in order?
cards.back: Pretrain, then supervised fine-tune, then train a reward model on human preference pairs, then optimize the policy (e.g., PPO) against it.

cards.front: DPO vs RLHF?
cards.back: DPO optimizes the preference objective directly from preference pairs - no separate reward model, no RL loop.

cards.front: What is reward hacking?
cards.back: The model games the reward signal instead of the real goal - why alignment needs evaluation blind-spot checks.

cards.back: Why pretraining is not alignment: from base model to instruction-following assistant; The RLHF pipeline: preference pairs, reward models, and PPO optimization; DPO and the preference-optimization family: alignment without a separate reward model; GRPO and RLVR: training on verifiable rewards for math, code, and tool use; Reasoning models and inference-time compute: longer chains of thought as a trained behavior; Reward hacking, KL drift, and evaluation blind spots: how alignment quietly fails.

cards.front: What is KL drift in alignment, and why penalize it?

cards.front: What are verifiable rewards (RLVR/GRPO)?
cards.back: Training on rewards checked programmatically - math answers, code passing tests - instead of a learned reward model. Sidesteps the RM bottleneck wherever ground truth exists.

notes.body: Alignment is an active research area, not a solved checklist — RLHF, DPO, and RLVR are current best practices as of 2026-10-07, not final answers. Preference data encodes whose preferences; 'aligned' always means aligned-to-someone. This module confers no certificate; the durable lesson is the failure-mode literacy: proxies get gamed, evaluations have blind spots, and the work is never 'done'.

cards.back: Dense vectors where semantic similarity becomes distance - similarity search finds the relevant chunks.

cards.front: What is BPE tokenization?
cards.back: Byte-pair encoding: repeatedly merges the most frequent character pairs - subword units balancing vocabulary size and coverage.

cards.front: The distributional hypothesis?
cards.back: Words appearing in similar contexts have similar meanings - the basis of Word2Vec and GloVe.

cards.front: Static vs contextual embeddings?
cards.back: Static: one vector per word (Word2Vec). Contextual: the vector depends on surrounding words - the transformer era.

cards.front: Why is subword tokenization the standard?

notes.title: Honesty note
Worked example: Which of the following is a topic covered in "Classic NLP with NLTK"?
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Classic NLP with NLTK, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

The failure catalog comes up front, because the demos never show the loop that wouldn't stop.

notes.body: MCP is a 2024-era open standard (as of 2026-10-07) — young enough that the ecosystem is still forming, which cuts both ways: momentum plus churn. A protocol standardizes the wire, not the trust — authorization and scoping remain your job. This module confers no certificate; the durable skill is the layer thinking: tools/data vs agent-messaging, standard vs bespoke.

notes.title: Worked example: In MCP, who calls whom?
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In The Protocol Layer: MCP and Agent Interoperability, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
Framework vocabulary. Frameworks package patterns; the patterns are the real curriculum.
- **Chains** — Sequenced model/tool calls with data passing between steps. LangChain's original composition unit — pipelines of LLM operations.
- **LCEL** — LangChain Expression Language: declarative chain composition with pipe operators. Chains as dataflow you can read.
- **LangChain agents** — Model-driven tool selection within the LangChain ecosystem: executors, toolkits, callbacks. The packaged ReAct loop.
- **AutoGen** — Conversable agents: multi-agent teams coordinating through conversation. Roles, group chat, human-in-the-loop hooks — the collaboration framework.
- **Conversable agents** — Agents as dialogue participants with system messages, code execution, and reply logic. Conversation as the coordination protocol.
- **Memory and state** — Conversation history, summaries, and external stores across turns. What the agent 'remembers' is an engineering choice with cost implications.
- **Callbacks / tracing** — Hooks observing every step: LangChain callbacks, AutoGen logging. The observability both frameworks provide — use it.
- **Evaluations for agents** — Task success, trajectory checks, cost/latency, human review. Framework demos rarely include evals; production requires them.
- **Framework vs hand-rolled** — Frameworks buy speed and ecosystem; hand-rolled buys control and debuggability. Simple agents often want the loop; complex ones may want the framework.
- **Abstraction risk** — Framework magic hiding the loop: when behavior surprises you, read down to the actual prompts and calls. The framework is not the agent.

cards.front: Compaction vs. clearing: when do you use each?
cards.back: Clearing wipes context between independent tasks. Compaction summarizes a long, still-relevant session into a shorter one that preserves state. Clear when the task changes; compact when the context outgrows the window but the work continues.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
Responsible-AI vocabulary. Principles first, then the machinery that implements them.
- **Fairness** — Systems shouldn't produce discriminatory outcomes across groups. The exam's scenarios test recognition of bias risks — and the honest caveat: fairness has competing definitions.
- **Reliability and safety** — Systems should behave consistently and avoid harmful outputs. Testing, red-teaming, and monitoring are the implementation.
- **Privacy and security** — Protecting data used and produced: no training-data leakage, proper access controls. The principle behind data-handling questions.
- **Transparency** — People should understand AI's role in decisions affecting them: disclosures, explanations, documentation. The 'human in the loop' family.
- **Accountability** — Humans own the outcomes: governance, oversight, and answerability for deployed systems. The principle that outlives every exam.
- **Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard** — The company's framework translating principles into engineering requirements: assessments, testing, and deployment gates.
- **Content filters** — Input/output filtering for harmful categories. The implemented control behind safety scenarios — configured, not magical.
- **Harm identification** — The exam skill: given a scenario, name the potential harms (bias, misinformation, over-reliance, privacy). Practice it as pattern recognition with real stakes.
- **Human oversight** — Keeping humans in consequential decisions: review, appeal, override. The accountability principle made operational.
- **Beyond the exam** — These obligations don't expire with the certification: fairness audits, safety testing, and documentation are production engineering.

Grading bar: any consequential system without a human-oversight design fails — and the audit must name what the mitigations don't cover.

notes.title: Honesty note
Worked example: Which of the following is a topic covered in "ML Systems Design"?
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In ML Systems Design, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

cards.back: Shadow: the new model scores live traffic without serving. Canary: a small traffic slice. Blue-green: full cutover with instant rollback.

cards.back: Batch: score many inputs at once, high throughput. Online: score one request at a time, low latency - the batching math decides.

notes.title: Concepts
Hands-on procedure
notes.code:
# Batching math, sketched
# throughput = batch_size / (fixed_overhead + batch_size * per_item)
# As batch grows, fixed_overhead amortizes -> throughput rises,
# but the first item waits for the batch -> p99 latency rises.
# Production setting: the knee of that curve, not the max.

notes.title: Project brief
Honesty note
notes.body: Serving is where ML meets operations reality: the best model that can't meet its SLO is the wrong model. Load tests on synthetic traffic lie politely — replay production shapes. This module confers no certificate; the durable skill is the latency budget discipline: measured, alerted, and honest.

notes.title: Worked example: Which of the following is a topic covered in "Model Serving and…
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Model Serving and Deployment Patterns, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
Cost/latency vocabulary. Every optimization attacks the dominant term — find it first.
- **Inference cost anatomy** — GPU-hours (compute), tokens (LLM billing), requests (overhead). Decompose first; the dominant term dictates the optimization.
- **Batching** — Amortizing fixed costs over many items. The throughput lever — with the latency tradeoff from the serving module.
- **Caching** — Storing repeated computations: exact-match caches, semantic caches, KV-cache reuse. The cheapest optimization when queries repeat.
- **Quantization for serving** — Lower-precision weights (8-bit down to sub-4-bit): smaller, faster, cheaper — with quality tradeoffs measured, not assumed.
- **Pruning / distillation (glance)** — Removing weights or training smaller mimics. The model-compression family beyond quantization — quality-measured, always.
- **Usage metering** — Per-tenant, per-feature, per-request accounting. You can't guardrail what you don't measure.
- **Cost guardrails** — Budgets, rate limits, and kill switches per tenant/feature. The multi-tenant defense against one user's bill becoming everyone's.
- **Right-sizing hardware** — Matching GPU/CPU to the workload: smaller models on cheaper hardware often win on cost-per-request. The 'when a smaller model wins' analysis.
- **The triangle** — Latency, throughput, cost: improve one, pay in the others. Every serving decision sits somewhere in this triangle — place it deliberately.
- **Unit economics** — Cost per request, per user, per task: the numbers the business actually feels. Engineering serves these, not FLOPs.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.code:
# Cost anatomy, worked sketch
# per_request = gpu_hours_per_req * $/gpu_hr + tokens_per_req * $/token
# Find the dominant term FIRST. Then:
#  - dominant = tokens   -> caching, smaller model, shorter contexts
#  - dominant = gpu-hours -> batching, quantization, right-sizing
#  - dominant = requests  -> batching, fewer round trips

cards.front: Why evaluate the trajectory, not just the final answer?
cards.back: A right answer via a wrong path is a landmine: tool misuse, hallucinated intermediate steps, or lucky guesses all pass an outcome check and fail in production. Trajectory eval scores each step against the expected path.

cards.back: Recorded good agent runs kept as regression sets - future changes must not break them.

cards.front: Name the key topics of "Agent Trajectory Evaluation".

notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In Agent Trajectory Evaluation, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

**Problem.** Point-in-time correctness prevents:

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Training features must reflect only data known at that timestamp.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
Data-centric vocabulary. The thesis: model performance is often a data problem wearing a model costume.
- **Data-centric thesis** — Fix the data before touching the model: labels, coverage, consistency. Most 'model problems' are data problems — verify before architecting.
- **Annotation pipelines** — Guidelines, training, agreement measurement, adjudication, quality sampling: human-feedback pipelines producing LLM-grade datasets. Infrastructure, not crowdsourcing.
- **Label quality** — Agreement rates, adjudication processes, edge-case handling. Noisy labels bound model performance — measure the noise before blaming the model.
- **Active learning** — Labeling the most informative examples first (uncertainty, diversity sampling). The labeling budget spent where it moves the metric.
- **Data versioning** — Immutable dataset versions with lineage: this model trained on that data snapshot. Git-for-data workflows making 'which data' answerable.
- **Lineage (data)** — From raw sources through cleaning through training: the provenance graph. Debugging 'why does the model do that' starts here.
- **Synthetic data** — Generated training examples: useful for rare cases and augmentation, dangerous as a primary source. Validate what it invents — against real data.
- **Data augmentation (revisited)** — Transformations expanding training coverage. The cheap data-centric win — with the label-preservation rule from the vision module.
- **Unstructured data engineering** — Raw documents → ML-ready sets: extraction, chunking, dedup, quality filtering. The pipeline feeding every LLM project.
- **Dataset audits** — Systematic checks: coverage, balance, leakage, bias, quality samples. The audit before the training run — cheap compared to training on garbage.

Grading bar: any model-architecture change in the report gets questioned — this is the data module, and the gains must come from data.

cards.front: What is the defining constraint of on-device inference?
cards.back: The resource envelope: memory, compute, battery, and thermal limits fixed at ship time. Everything else - quantization, pruning, distillation, smaller architectures - is a negotiation with that envelope.

cards.front: Why quantize models for serving?
cards.back: Lower precision (8-bit down to sub-4-bit) cuts memory and latency - with quality tradeoffs measured honestly.

cards.front: What is ONNX for?
cards.back: Open model interchange: export once, run across frameworks and runtimes such as ONNX Runtime.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
Capstone-framing vocabulary. Week one decides week twelve.
- **Problem worth solving** — Scoped enough to finish, substantial enough to matter, demonstrable in ten minutes. The three filters every capstone idea passes — or doesn't.
- **Success metrics first** — Defined and agreed before modeling: the number that decides 'done'. Metrics chosen after modeling are rationalizations.
- **Data audit** — What exists, what's missing, quality, licensing, access: the inventory before the commitment. No data, no project — decide now.
- **Feasibility baseline** — The simplest end-to-end attempt proving the problem is solvable with available data. De-risks the project before the real work.
- **Scoping to finish** — Milestones with dates, explicit cut lines, and a minimum viable demo defined upfront. Ambition scheduled is achievable; ambition assumed is not.
- **Stakeholder agreement** — Who decides 'good enough': you, a reviewer, a hiring manager. Aligned expectations prevent week-twelve disputes.
- **Risk register** — Named risks (data access, compute, scope creep) with mitigations. The honest planning artifact — revisited, not filed.
- **The demo test** — 'Can I demo this in ten minutes to a hiring manager?' If no, re-scope. The portfolio is the point.
- **Literature grounding** — What exists already: prior work, baselines, tools. Originality is optional; awareness is not.
- **Ethical pre-check** — Harms, biases, and misuse potential considered before building. The responsible-AI module's lessons, applied to your own project.

notes.body: Capstone framing document: the chosen problem with the three-filter justification, agreed success metrics, full data audit, feasibility baseline results, scoped milestones with cut lines and dates, risk register, minimum viable demo definition, literature grounding, and the ethical pre-check. Grading bar: I review the framing as a hiring manager would — vague metrics, unaudited data, or missing cut lines send it back. This document gates the entire capstone path.

**Problem.** Which of the following is a topic covered in "End-to-End Build"?

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Knowing when to stop tuning
- **Why:** "Knowing when to stop tuning" is listed among this module's topics; the other options come from different modules.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *"Knowing when to stop tuning" is listed among this module's topics; the other options come from different modules.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Concepts
Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Evaluate your capstone like an adversary. The evidence bar is the grade.
1. **Lock the protocol.** Define the eval protocol before running: data, metrics, slices, ablations — written down. Protocol after results is rationalization.
2. **Evaluate held-out.** Run the full system on untouched test data; report with the protocol. The headline numbers, earned.
3. **Slice it.** Break results by meaningful subgroups; find the worst slice. The slice that embarrasses you is the most valuable finding.
4. **Ablate it.** Remove each major component; measure the delta. Components that don't move the number get questioned — 'what actually helped', answered.
5. **Stress it.** Edge cases, noisy inputs, distribution shift, adversarial-ish probes: find the breaking points deliberately. Document each with the failure signature.
6. **Limit it.** Write the limits section: what it can't do, where it breaks, what you'd need to fix it. The most trusted section — write it like one.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Capstone evaluation report: held-out results with documented protocol, slice analysis with the worst slice investigated, ablations for every major component, stress-test results with breaking points, the honest limits section, and comparisons against baselines run identically. Grading bar: unevaluated claims fail — 'it works well' without the evidence bar (held-out, slices, ablations, stress, limits) is a demo, not a result.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
MLOps-lite vocabulary. Production discipline at solo-engineer scale.
- **Notebook to service** — The packaging path: dependencies pinned, inference code extracted, container or endpoint. The graduation from exploration to operation.
- **Serving API design** — Clean request/response contracts: versioned endpoints, validated inputs, meaningful errors. The interface others build against.
- **Input monitoring** — Watching what the model receives: schema checks, distribution summaries, anomaly flags. Garbage in, caught early.
- **Prediction monitoring** — Tracking output distributions for drift without labels. The early warning from the production path, at solo scale.
- **Drift at small scale** — Simple statistical checks and volume thresholds instead of platform tooling. Appropriate monitoring, not enterprise theater.
- **Retraining triggers (lite)** — Calendar plus performance-threshold triggers with a runbook. The 'when' answered with a checklist, not a platform.
- **Cost awareness** — Serving cost tracked per request/day: the number that decides whether the demo stays up. Hobby budgets need engineering too.
- **Rollback (lite)** — Previous version kept deployable: the one-command revert. Solo-engineer safety net.
- **Documentation for operators** — The runbook: deploy, monitor, retrain, roll back, costs. Future-you is the operator — write for them.
- **Demo reliability** — The serving bar for a portfolio piece: it works when the hiring manager clicks. Reliability is the feature.

notes.title: Honesty note
Worked example: Which of the following is a topic covered in "The Portfolio Piece"?
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
AI systems fail in ways traditional software doesn't. In The Portfolio Piece, these are the recurring traps:
- **Prompt-and-pray.** Shipping LLM behavior with no evals. If you can't measure it, you can't improve it — build the eval harness before you tune the prompt.
- **No data versioning.** Retraining on a dataset you can't reproduce. Version data, code, and config together or your results are anecdotes.
- **Ignoring cost and latency.** A brilliant pipeline nobody can afford to run is a prototype. Track tokens, compute, and p99 latency from the first experiment.
- **Training-serving skew.** Features computed differently in training and serving silently rot the model. One code path for features, used in both places.
- **Shipping without red-teaming.** Adversarial testing isn't optional for systems that talk to users. Probe for jailbreaks, injection, and data exfiltration before launch, not after.
- **Eval on vibes.** 'Looks good to me' on five examples. Build a graded eval set with clear pass criteria and run it on every change.

cards.front: The autonomy ceiling for an agent design?
cards.back: The as-of dated P50 time horizon for your model class — subtasks longer than it need decomposition or human-in-the-loop.

cards.front: P50 horizon, fitted how?
cards.back: Logistic curve of model success vs human task length; the 50% crossing. ~7-month doubling (195.8 days, 2019–2025).

cards.front: TH1.1's update for engineers?
cards.back: Post-2023 doubling 130.8 days — ceilings move faster than the long-run trend; re-check quarterly.

cards.front: A vendor claims 16-hour autonomy. Your response?
cards.back: Show the curve, the suite, the interval — METR warns >16h measurements are unreliable; verify on your own tasks.

cards.front: The one-line design rule?
cards.back: No subtask past the measured P50 without a checkpoint. The ceiling is a boundary, not a target.

cards.front: Why must a horizon value always carry a date?
cards.back: Horizons move in months (post-2023 doubling ~131 days) — an undated ceiling is a rumor, not an engineering input.

cards.front: What does the time-horizon metric NOT claim?
cards.back: It is a fitted reliability boundary, not a capability certificate. It doesn't promise success on YOUR task, ignores tool-access and prompting differences, and ages as models improve - verify against the critical-reading checklist.

cards.front: How do you scope an agent deployment with the horizon?
cards.back: Decompose the job so the longest unsupervised subtask sits under the as-of P50 horizon. Anything longer gets human checkpoints or tighter decomposition - the horizon is a scoping tool, not a marketing number.

notes.body: Set an autonomy ceiling for a real agent design. Pick an agent use case you care about (coding assistant, ops runbook runner, research helper). What endures: the discipline — never design past a measured ceiling on a vendor's word alone; verify on your own tasks, with your own baselines.

scriptLabs.title: Vectorize a loop with NumPy
scriptLabs.brief: Python loops over a million elements are the classic AI-engineering bottleneck. Compute the mean of squares without a single Python loop.
scriptLabs.starter:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.random(1_000_000)
# TODO: mean of squares, no Python loop
scriptLabs.hint: Elementwise power with ** 2 is vectorized; np.mean reduces the result. Two operations, zero loops.
scriptLabs.solution:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.random(1_000_000)
result = np.mean(a ** 2)
print(result)

scriptLabs.title: Keep preprocessing inside the fold
scriptLabs.brief: Scaling before the split leaks. Build a scikit-learn pipeline so the scaler is fit inside each cross-validation fold, then score it honestly.
scriptLabs.starter:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
# TODO: pipeline + 5-fold CV on (X, y)
scriptLabs.hint: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(...)) then cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5). The scaler refits per fold automatically.
scriptLabs.solution:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5)
print(scores.mean())

scriptLabs.title: Write one PyTorch training step
scriptLabs.brief: Every PyTorch project shares one loop. Write a single training step by hand: forward, loss, backward, step - with gradients cleared first.
scriptLabs.starter:
import torch
# model, criterion, optimizer, xb, yb are provided
# TODO: one full training step
scriptLabs.hint: Order matters: zero_grad, forward pass, compute loss, backward, step. Forgetting zero_grad accumulates stale gradients.
scriptLabs.solution:
optimizer.zero_grad()
outputs = model(xb)
loss = criterion(outputs, yb)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

vec = TfidfVectorizer().fit(docs + [query])
D = vec.transform(docs)
q = vec.transform([query])
scores = cosine_similarity(q, D)[0]
best = docs[int(scores.argmax())]
print(best, round(float(scores.max()), 3))

scenarios.title: The 99% model that fails in production
scenarios.context: Your classifier scores 99% in validation but 61% on live data. Something is wrong with the evaluation, not the world.

steps.prompt: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Data leakage - preprocessing fit on the full dataset before the split
options.why: Scaling or encoding fit before splitting leaks test information into training - validation scores become fiction.

options.text: The model is underfitting
options.why: Underfitting shows low scores everywhere, not a 99-to-61 collapse.

options.text: The learning rate is too high
options.why: A bad learning rate hurts training too - it does not create a validation/production gap.

options.text: Too little training data
options.why: Small data hurts all scores roughly equally; the gap pattern points to leakage.

options.text: Put every preprocessing step inside a pipeline, inside the cross-validation fold
options.why: Pipelines refit preprocessing per fold - no information crosses the train/validation boundary.

options.text: Collect more data and retrain the same way
options.why: More data with the same leakage just produces more confident fiction.

options.text: Switch to a deeper neural network
options.why: Model complexity does not fix an evaluation methodology bug.

options.text: Tune hyperparameters on the test set
options.why: Tuning on the test set is itself leakage - the test set must stay held out.

steps.prompt: How do you verify the fix worked?

options.text: Evaluate once on a held-out test set that never touched training or tuning
options.why: A truly held-out test set is the only honest estimate of production performance.

options.text: Re-run the same cross-validation and trust it
options.why: CV you already tuned against is optimistic - you need untouched data.

options.text: Check training accuracy
options.why: Training accuracy measures memorization, not generalization.

options.text: Ask stakeholders if the number looks right
options.why: Plausibility is not evidence - measure on held-out data.

scenarios.title: Grounding answers in changing product docs
scenarios.context: Support needs an assistant that answers from product documentation that updates weekly. You must choose the architecture.

steps.prompt: RAG or fine-tuning for weekly-changing docs?

options.text: RAG - retrieve the current docs at query time, then generate grounded on them
options.why: RAG handles frequently changing knowledge without retraining; fine-tuning bakes in knowledge that goes stale.

options.text: Fine-tune weekly on the new docs
options.why: Weekly fine-tuning is expensive, slow, and still cannot cite sources.

options.text: Prompt the base model harder
options.why: Prompting cannot inject knowledge the model never saw.

options.text: Train a model from scratch on the docs
options.why: Massively disproportionate cost for a retrieval problem.

steps.prompt: Answers must cite their sources. Which chunking choice helps?

options.text: Parent-child chunks: retrieve small passages, cite the parent section
options.why: Small chunks retrieve precisely; parent context keeps citations traceable to the real document section.

options.text: One giant chunk per document
options.why: Giant chunks dilute retrieval precision and waste context.

options.text: No chunking - embed whole PDFs
options.why: Whole-document embeddings blur the specific passage the answer needs.

options.text: Random chunk boundaries
options.why: Arbitrary boundaries split coherent passages and break citation quality.

steps.prompt: How do you evaluate the system honestly?

options.text: A golden question-answer set scored for groundedness and citation accuracy
options.why: Fixed evals with groundedness checks measure what matters: correct, cited answers - not vibes.

options.text: Ask the team if answers look good
options.why: Eyeballing does not catch regressions or hallucinations systematically.

options.text: Count how fast it responds
options.why: Latency matters, but speed says nothing about correctness.

options.text: Trust the demo - it worked once
options.why: One good demo is not evidence; evals are.

scenarios.title: The prediction-drift alert fires
scenarios.context: Monitoring flags prediction drift on your production model: the output distribution shifted this week. Revenue-facing decisions depend on it.

options.text: Whether the input data distribution shifted (data drift) or the input-output relationship changed (concept drift)
options.why: The distinction decides the fix: shifted inputs may need pipeline repair; a changed relationship needs retraining on fresh labels.

options.text: Restart the serving containers
options.why: Restarts fix infrastructure, not statistical drift.

options.text: Immediately retrain on all historical data
options.why: Retraining without diagnosing wastes the chance to find the real cause - and may bake in the problem.

options.text: Disable monitoring to stop the alerts
options.why: Silencing the smoke detector during a fire.

steps.prompt: Diagnosis: concept drift - the relationship itself changed. What now?

options.text: Retrain on freshly labeled data reflecting the new relationship, with a holdout for validation
options.why: Concept drift means old labels encode the old world - only fresh labels teach the new one.

options.text: Keep the old model; drift always reverts
options.why: Hope is not a retraining trigger - evidence of reversion would be needed, and you have the opposite.

options.text: Tune hyperparameters on the old data
options.why: Hyperparameters cannot fix labels that describe a world that no longer exists.

options.text: Add more features from the same stale pipeline
options.why: More stale features do not repair a changed relationship.

steps.prompt: How do you ship the retrained model safely?

options.text: Shadow or canary deployment with a rollback plan before full cutover
options.why: Progressive delivery proves the new model on live traffic with a safe retreat - the production discipline.

options.text: Replace the model file directly in production
options.why: Big-bang swaps with no rollback turn every retrain into a gamble.

options.text: Ship it Friday evening to avoid traffic
options.why: Low traffic means slow detection of problems - and nobody around to roll back.

options.text: Skip evaluation; the training loss looked good
options.why: Training loss never validated a production model.

blocks.body: Autograd accumulates gradients via the chain rule over the computation graph. zero_grad() prevents accumulation across batches.
More data > augmentation > dropout/weight decay > smaller model > early stopping. Regularize in that order.
Loss explodes → LR too high. Loss flat → LR too low or bug. LR finder / warmup + cosine decay for transformers.
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V. Queries match keys; values get mixed by the match weights. √d scaling keeps softmax out of saturation.
H parallel attention heads in learned subspaces, concatenated and projected. Different heads learn different relations.
GPT: causal (left-to-right) masking, generative pretraining. BERT: bidirectional masking, masked-LM + NSP. One predicts next, the other fills blanks.
Attention is permutation-invariant, so position must be injected: sinusoidal, learned, RoPE, ALiBi. RoPE dominates modern LLMs.
Chinchilla: ~20 tokens per parameter is compute-optimal. Bigger isn't better — bigger *with enough data* is.

cheatSheets.title: RAG + vector search — the production pattern

blocks.body: Chunk (512–1024 tokens, overlap) → embed → index (HNSW) → retrieve top-k → rerank → generate with citations → evaluate.
recall@k and MRR on a golden set. If recall is bad, generation can't save you. Chunking strategy beats embedding model choice.
Lost in the middle (long contexts), stale index, chunk-boundary splits, prompt injection via retrieved docs. Cite sources; verify claims.
Stable facts the model knows → skip retrieval. Style/format → fine-tune. Changing facts + citations → RAG.
Golden prompts + rubrics; LLM-judge with human calibration; regression-gate every prompt/model change. Trajectory evals for agents (tool efficiency, not just success).
Input/output token pricing; cache prompts; route easy queries to small models; batch; distill. Measure $/task, not $/token.
Prompt injection, jailbreaks, data exfiltration via tools, insecure output handling. Treat model output as untrusted input to your system.
Model cards, data lineage, bias evals, human-in-the-loop for high-stakes decisions. 'AI proposes, human disposes.'

answerBank.q: What does this academy prepare you for?
answerBank.a: The full AI-engineer spine: Python, data science, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, NLP, agentic systems, Azure AI, and production MLOps - ending in one deployed capstone. Preparation only, conferring no certificate.

answerBank.q: Is this course affiliated with Microsoft or the bootcamp program it was distilled from?
answerBank.a: No. It is distilled from the public shape of a third-party Microsoft-ecosystem AI Engineer bootcamp program, with original exposition throughout - not affiliated with either, and vendor documentation is the anchor, never the copy.

answerBank.q: Does completing this academy confer a certificate?
answerBank.a: No. Preparation only - this course confers no certificate. Vendor certification exams are taken through the vendor's own portal.

answerBank.q: When should I choose RAG over fine-tuning?
answerBank.a: Choose RAG when knowledge updates frequently and answers must cite sources - retrieve, then generate. Choose fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA/QLoRA) when behavior must change permanently on stable data.
The distance between modeling and operating: a trained model is not a system. Production demands serving, monitoring, drift response, cost control, evaluation harnesses, and rollback plans.

answerBank.q: Which exam does the Azure path map to?
answerBank.a: Microsoft's AI-900 (Azure AI Fundamentals): the Azure AI service catalog, ML concepts in Microsoft's vocabulary, responsible AI, and cost/governance/compliance scenarios.

answerBank.q: How should I choose between RAG and fine-tuning?
answerBank.a: Ask three questions. Does the knowledge change? If yes, RAG — weights shouldn't chase moving facts. Do answers need citations? If yes, RAG — grounding is traceable. Do you need behavior or style internalized (tone, format, reasoning patterns)? That's fine-tuning's job. Then run both on the same task and measure: retrieval hit-rate and groundedness for RAG, task performance plus forgetting checks for the tuned model. The experiment decides; the heuristics just pick the starting lineup.

answerBank.q: My agent works in demos but loops and drifts in real tasks. What's the fix?
answerBank.a: Treat the loop as the system, not the model. Add a step budget with a loop breaker (progress detection, escalate-to-human), restate the goal with checkpoint summaries to fight drift, and bound tool capabilities with least privilege plus human gates on irreversible actions. Then instrument: log every iteration (thought, action, observation) and meter per-run cost. Most 'agent failures' are missing control flow, not missing intelligence — the fixes are engineering, and they're all in the agentic path's failure catalog.

answerBank.q: How do I know my evaluation numbers are honest?
answerBank.a: Run the checklist: test data untouched during development (no peeking), preprocessing inside the pipeline inside the fold (no leakage), metrics matched to the business cost of each error type (no accuracy-on-imbalance lies), intervals around the headline number (no naked point estimates), and ablations showing what actually helped. Then slice the results — the worst slice is usually the most informative. If any check fails, the number is a claim, not a result.

faq.q: How much math do I need before the PyTorch modules?
faq.a: Linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) + calculus (gradients) + probability. The course opens with exactly that spine — don't skip it; backprop is the chain rule.
PyTorch — it's the research and production default for new work (Hugging Face ecosystem, vLLM serving). The course commits to it throughout.

faq.q: When do I fine-tune vs use RAG vs prompt engineer?
faq.a: Prompt engineer first (cheapest). RAG for changing facts + citations. Fine-tune (LoRA) for style/format/domain idiom. Evaluate each step — most teams over-fine-tune.

faq.q: How do I evaluate an LLM feature honestly?
faq.a: Golden set + rubric + LLM judge calibrated against humans, regression-gated in CI. For agents, trajectory evals: tool calls, efficiency, safety — not just final answer.

faq.q: What's the cheapest way to serve a model?
faq.a: Quantized open-weight model on vLLM/Ollama for steady load; API for spiky load. Measure $/completed task including retries, and route easy queries to small models.

faq.q: Is the 'Attention Is All You Need' paper still worth reading?
faq.a: Yes — the original (arXiv 1706.03762) is short and the architecture diagram is the Rosetta stone for every transformer since. The course assigns it in the transformers module.

faq.q: How do I keep an agent from doing something destructive?
faq.a: Least-privilege tools, instruction hierarchy, output validation, max-step budgets, and human approval gates for irreversible actions. The safety module treats this as engineering, not vibes.

faq.q: What does 'no vendor affiliation' mean for Azure modules?
faq.a: The course teaches Azure AI services as *tools* with honest cost/lock-in analysis — it confers no certification and claims no partnership. Independent-prep framing throughout.

tips: Follow the guided path in order — each module unlocks the next. The sequence is the curriculum; skipping ahead breaks the chain.

studyGuide.title: Study guide: how to work IL-12
studyGuide.note: totalHours/totalMinutes are filled from module estimatedMinutes; declared hours are the honest rounded sum.
pacing: Weeks 1-3 — Foundations: prereq math primers, Python, NumPy/pandas, statistics for ML.
Weeks 4-8 — Classical ML: supervised, unsupervised, RL first contact, validation, features, metrics.
Weeks 9-13 — Deep learning: neural foundations, backprop, CNNs, sequences, regularization, PyTorch workflows.
Weeks 14-19 — Generative AI and NLP: transformers, RAG, vector DBs, fine-tuning, alignment, Hugging Face.
Weeks 20-24 — Agentic AI, Azure AI-900, production MLOps, and the 6-part capstone.
Final — Certification gates: clear the AWS MLA, Databricks, and TensorFlow gates twice before booking.
rules: Do the math primers before neural foundations.
Train every model yourself; never copy a trained artifact.
Clear each certification gate twice on separate days.
